units.title: Diagnostic Thinking: Assessing Model Health
units.description: Learn to look beyond R-squared. We dive into residual plots, p-values, and the F-test to determine if a model is trustworthy or misleading.

lectures.title: The Truth in the Residuals
lectures.description: Before trusting a single number, we look at the 'noise' left behind by the model. This lecture focuses on visualizing error patterns to identify fundamental model failures.

sessions.title: Anatomy of a Residual Plot
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to construct and interpret a residual plot as the primary diagnostic tool for regression. You will learn to recognize what a 'healthy' plot looks like—a random cloud of points—and why any discernible pattern signals a violation of model assumptions. This establishes the critical habit of visual verification before statistical reporting, which is essential for your goal of moving from intuition to professional practice.

tasks: Identify three common visual patterns in residual plots that indicate a bad model fit.
Sketch a residual plot for a model that has failed to capture a non-linear relationship.

keyPoints: Definition of a residual as the difference between observed and predicted values
Constructing the residual vs. fitted value scatterplot
The 'ideal' random distribution of residuals
Identifying non-linearity through curved residual patterns

sessions.title: Detecting Heteroscedasticity
sessions.description: In this session, we tackle the problem of 'unequal variance' or heteroscedasticity. You will learn to spot the classic 'funnel' shape in residual plots and understand why this makes your standard errors and p-values unreliable. This depth allows you to diagnose when a model is more certain about some predictions than others, a key step in building robust, professional-grade models.

tasks: Contrast a homoscedastic residual plot with a heteroscedastic one.
Explain why heteroscedasticity doesn't bias the coefficients but does break the hypothesis tests.

keyPoints: The constant variance assumption (homoscedasticity)
Visualizing the 'funnel' or 'megaphone' effect
Impact of heteroscedasticity on confidence intervals
Common causes of variance changes in real-world data

lectures.title: Statistical Significance and the P-Value Logic
lectures.description: We move from visual inspection to formal hypothesis testing to determine if the relationship we've found is real or just a coincidence of the data.

sessions.title: The Null Hypothesis for Regression Coefficients
sessions.description: This session introduces the formal logic of the T-test applied to regression coefficients. You will learn how to set up the null hypothesis (that the slope is zero) and how the T-statistic measures the distance between your observation and that 'nothing is happening' scenario. Mastering this logic is the bridge from simple data description to making statistically sound inferences about populations.

tasks: Formulate the null and alternative hypotheses for a specific slope coefficient.
Calculate a T-statistic given a coefficient estimate and its standard error.

keyPoints: Conceptualizing the null hypothesis Beta=0
The T-statistic as a signal-to-noise ratio
Standard error of the slope coefficient
Degrees of freedom in a linear model context

sessions.title: Interpreting P-Values Without the Myths
sessions.description: You will learn the precise definition of a P-value and, more importantly, what it is not. This session clarifies the 0.05 threshold and teaches you how to interpret 'significance' in the context of the effect size. This prevents common beginner pitfalls and ensures your diagnostic thinking is aligned with modern academic and professional standards.

tasks: Draft a one-sentence interpretation of a p-value of 0.03 for a specific variable.
Explain the difference between statistical significance and practical importance.

keyPoints: Probability of observing data under the null hypothesis
The arbitrary nature of alpha thresholds (0.05)
The relationship between p-values and sample size
Why a low p-value doesn't prove the model is 'good'

lectures.title: Evaluating the Model as a Whole
lectures.description: While individual variables might be significant, we need a way to test if the entire collection of predictors provides real value.

sessions.title: The Global F-Test
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to perform the F-test to assess the overall model significance. You will learn how this 'omnibus' test compares your model against a 'mean-only' model to see if your predictors collectively reduce the error significantly. This provides a 'gatekeeper' check that prevents you from interpreting individual coefficients in a model that is essentially white noise.

tasks: Compare the utility of a T-test versus an F-test in Multiple Linear Regression.
Identify a scenario where individual variables are insignificant but the F-test is significant.

keyPoints: The Null Hypothesis for the global F-test
Partitioning variance: SSR vs SSE
Mean Squares and the F-ratio calculation
Interpreting the F-statistic p-value

sessions.title: The R-Squared Trap
sessions.description: You will learn the definition of R-squared and Adjusted R-squared, specifically focusing on why a high R-squared can be deceptive. This session teaches you how to use R-squared as a measure of fit while maintaining the 'diagnostic eye' needed to spot overfitting or omitted variable bias. This nuance is what separates a systematic master from a novice practitioner.

tasks: Calculate Adjusted R-squared and explain why it penalizes adding useless variables.
Provide an example of a high R-squared model that is fundamentally flawed.

keyPoints: Proportion of variance explained
The problem of R-squared always increasing with more variables
Adjusted R-squared formula and logic
Limitations of R-squared as a measure of 'truth'

lectures.title: Assumptions and Influential Points
lectures.description: We conclude the diagnostic unit by checking the distribution of our errors and identifying data points that might be pulling the line too hard.

sessions.title: Normality of Residuals
sessions.description: This session explores the assumption that residuals are normally distributed. You will learn to use Q-Q plots and histograms to check this assumption and understand why it matters for the validity of your hypothesis tests. This completes your diagnostic toolkit for basic linear models, ensuring your conclusions are mathematically sound.

tasks: Interpret a Q-Q plot showing heavy tails.
Discuss how the Central Limit Theorem helps when residuals aren't perfectly normal.

keyPoints: The Normal distribution of error terms
Visualizing normality with Histograms and Q-Q plots
Consequences of non-normality on inference
Identifying skewness in residuals

sessions.title: Outliers, Leverage, and Influence
sessions.description: You will learn the difference between an outlier (y-direction) and a high-leverage point (x-direction), and how to identify points that have a disproportionate influence on your model's results. This session teaches you how to maintain the integrity of your model by investigating these 'strange' points rather than just deleting them. This is a crucial skill for dealing with the 'messy dataset' project later in the course.

tasks: Define leverage and influence in your own words.
Sketch a scenario where a single outlier significantly changes the slope of the regression line.

keyPoints: Defining Outliers vs High Leverage points
Cook's Distance as a measure of Influence
The 'leave-one-out' intuition for influence
Ethical and practical considerations of removing data points

projects.stage_description: Perform a rigorous health check on your MLR model by generating residual plots to check for heteroscedasticity and calculating P-values for each coefficient to identify non-significant predictors.
projects.deliverable_increment: A diagnostic suite including a Residual vs. Fitted plot, a Q-Q plot, and a table of P-values/T-statistics.

exams.title: Model Health Diagnostic Exam
exams.goal: Verify the learner's ability to interpret residual plots, perform hypothesis tests for significance, and assess overall model validity through global metrics.
sections: Comprehensive evaluation of diagnostic visualization (residual plots, Q-Q plots), interpretation of p-values and F-tests, and the critical assessment of R-squared vs. Adjusted R-squared.
successCriteria: Correctly identify violations of assumptions (heteroscedasticity, non-linearity) from visual plots.
Accurately interpret the p-value for a specific coefficient and the global F-test.
Explain the necessity of Adjusted R-squared in multiple regression.
Distinguish between outliers and influential points and their impact on the model.

units.title: From Math to Software: Mastering Model Outputs
units.description: A hands-on walkthrough of standardized output tables from tools like R (tidymodels) and Python (statsmodels) to bridge the gap to practice.

lectures.title: Anatomy of a Regression Summary
lectures.description: This lecture demystifies the dense text output generated by statistical software, teaching you how to quickly locate and verify the most critical numbers.

sessions.title: The Big Three: Coefficients, SE, and T-Stats
sessions.description: In this session, you will learn to navigate the central table of a regression output, focusing on the estimate, standard error, and the resulting t-statistic. You will gain the ability to explain how these three numbers work together to determine the precision of a variable's effect. This serves your goal of moving from theoretical math to practitioner-level interpretation by translating the OLS formulas from Unit 2 into software-generated reality.

tasks: Locate the coefficient for a specific predictor in a provided screenshot of a statsmodels table.
Calculate a t-statistic manually using the provided Estimate and Std. Error values.

keyPoints: The 'Estimate' as the calculated slope
Standard Error as the measure of uncertainty
The T-statistic as a signal-to-noise ratio
Mapping software labels to mathematical symbols

sessions.title: The Confidence Interval: Range of Plausibility
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to interpret the 95% confidence interval columns found in modern software summaries. You will be able to determine whether an effect is not only statistically significant but also practically meaningful based on its range of likely values. This bridges the gap between 'knowing a number' and 'trusting a range,' a vital skill for robust modeling.

tasks: Identify if a coefficient is significant by checking if the confidence interval crosses zero.
Compare two models' intervals to determine which estimate is more precise.

keyPoints: Definition of the 95% Confidence Interval
The relationship between SE and interval width
Zero-crossing as a test for significance
Interpretation of interval bounds in real-world units

lectures.title: Global Metrics: Is the Model Any Good?
lectures.description: Moving beyond individual variables, this lecture focuses on the 'Top-Level' metrics that describe the overall health and fit of the entire regression model.

sessions.title: Deconstructing R-Squared and Adjusted R-Squared
sessions.description: This session explains the difference between the standard R-squared and the Adjusted R-squared reported in software summaries. You will learn why Adjusted R-squared is the more honest metric in Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) and how to use it to detect 'overfitting' by adding useless variables. Understanding this prevents you from falling into the common beginner trap of trusting a high but inflated R-squared value.

tasks: Compare R-squared vs. Adjusted R-squared for a model with 20 predictors.
Predict how R-squared changes when a random noise variable is added to the model.

keyPoints: R-squared as proportion of variance explained
The penalty for complexity in Adjusted R-squared
When to prefer Adjusted over Multiple R-squared
Signs of an over-parameterized model

sessions.title: Information Criteria: Intro to AIC and BIC
sessions.description: You will be introduced to AIC and BIC, the metrics used for model comparison that you will see in every professional stats summary. You will gain the ability to use these scores to select the 'best' model among several candidates by balancing fit against complexity. This prepares you for the model selection techniques that will be critical in Unit 7's discussion on regularization.

tasks: Rank three different model summaries from best to worst using only AIC values.
Identify which criterion (AIC or BIC) provides a harsher penalty for model size.

keyPoints: The intuition of 'Information Loss'
AIC vs. BIC: Different penalty strengths
The 'Lower is Better' rule of thumb
Using IC for non-nested model comparison

lectures.title: Workflow Integration: From Code to Insights
lectures.description: This lecture focuses on the practical execution in Python and R, ensuring you can generate these summaries yourself and extract the data programmatically.

sessions.title: Generating Reports in Python and R
sessions.description: In this session, you will see the specific code snippets required to run a regression and print a summary using Python's statsmodels and R's tidymodels. You will be able to set up a basic modeling workflow and interpret the resulting 'tidy' data frames. This directly supports your goal of becoming a production-ready practitioner by moving from conceptual understanding to executable code.

tasks: Write the line of code in Python to extract the p-values from a fitted model object.
Identify the R function used to turn a messy summary into a clean tibble.

keyPoints: Statsmodels OLS .summary() output
Tidymodels broom::tidy() and glance()
Extracting specific coefficients programmatically
Comparison of software-specific formatting

sessions.title: Standard Errors and Robust Options
sessions.description: This session introduces the concept of 'Robust' standard errors, which often appear as options in software like Stata or R. You will learn why a practitioner might click the 'robust' button and how it changes the interpretation of the output table. This provides a bridge to Unit 6, where we deal with real-world data that violates standard OLS assumptions.

tasks: Spot the difference in SE values between a standard OLS run and a robust HC3 run.
Explain when to use robust errors based on a residual plot.

keyPoints: Limitations of standard OLS SE estimates
What 'Heteroscedasticity-Consistent' (HC) means
Software flags for robust estimation
Impact on p-values and significance

exams.title: Unit 5 Comprehensive Assessment: Interpreting Software Summaries
exams.goal: Evaluate the learner's ability to extract, interpret, and compare regression models using standardized software outputs from statsmodels and tidymodels.
sections: A comprehensive evaluation covering coefficient interpretation, global fit metrics (R-squared/AIC), and programmatic extraction of model statistics from summary tables.
successCriteria: Correctly identify p-values and confidence intervals in a sample output table.
Explain the difference between Multiple and Adjusted R-squared in a multi-predictor context.
Choose the superior model based on AIC/BIC scores.
State the correct interpretation of a coefficient from a 'tidy' model summary.

units.title: Real-World Complexity: Collinearity and Interactions
units.description: We tackle the problems that arise with messy, real-world data, including variables that move together and effects that depend on one another.

lectures.title: The Problem of Overlapping Information: Multicollinearity
lectures.description: This lecture explains what happens when predictors are highly correlated and why this destabilizes our model estimates.

sessions.title: The Geometry of Redundancy
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to visualize multicollinearity as overlapping vectors in high-dimensional space. You will understand why the model struggles to assign 'credit' to individual variables when they move in unison, which is a critical foundation for building interpretable and stable models.

tasks: Identify perfectly collinear variables in a sample data frame.
Sketch the projection of a response variable onto two nearly parallel predictor vectors.

keyPoints: Definition of multicollinearity
Redundancy in feature spaces
Uncertainty in coefficient estimation
Impact on standard errors

sessions.title: Detecting Hidden Correlation with VIF
sessions.description: This session introduces the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) as a mathematical diagnostic for redundancy. You will learn how to calculate and interpret VIF scores to decide when a variable must be removed or combined, moving you closer to producing production-ready, reliable regression models.

tasks: Calculate VIF for a simple three-variable system.
Determine the exclusion threshold for a real-world messy dataset summary.

keyPoints: R-squared of predictors vs predictors
VIF calculation formula
Rule-of-thumb thresholds (5 and 10)
Strategies for dropping variables

lectures.title: Synergy in Data: Modeling Interactions
lectures.description: We move beyond additive models to explore cases where the effect of one variable depends on the level of another.

sessions.title: The Intuition of Synergy
sessions.description: This session teaches you the conceptual difference between additive effects and interaction effects using real-world examples like dosage and body weight. You will learn to recognize when simple addition fails to capture the true relationship in your data, which is essential for capturing complex business or scientific phenomena.

tasks: Compare additive vs interaction predictions for a specific data point.
Identify real-world examples where 'it depends' logic applies.

keyPoints: Limitations of additive models
Conceptual definition of interaction
Visualizing non-parallel slopes
The 'It Depends' principle

sessions.title: Mathematical Formulation of Interaction Terms
sessions.description: This session covers the technical side of adding product terms (X1 * X2) to your regression equation. You will gain the ability to derive the changing slope of one variable relative to another, enabling you to build more sophisticated models that outperform basic linear approximations.

tasks: Write out the full regression equation for a model with two continuous predictors and their interaction.
Calculate the partial derivative of the response with respect to one variable.

keyPoints: Product terms in equations
Interaction between continuous variables
Interaction between categorical and continuous variables
Interpretation of the interaction coefficient

lectures.title: Interpreting Complex Models in Practice
lectures.description: A practical focus on how to explain interaction coefficients and multicollinearity impacts to stakeholders.

sessions.title: Centering Variables for Clarity
sessions.description: This session teaches you the technique of mean-centering continuous variables before creating interactions. You will learn how this reduces structural multicollinearity and makes the 'main effect' coefficients much easier to interpret, a vital skill for presenting clear results to non-technical audiences.

tasks: Transform a raw dataset into mean-centered variables.
Re-interpret a coefficient from a centered model.

keyPoints: Structural vs data multicollinearity
Mean-centering mechanics
Improvement in coefficient interpretability
Effect on the intercept

sessions.title: The Hierarchy Principle
sessions.description: This session explains why you must almost always include main effects when including an interaction term. You will learn the 'Hierarchy Principle' of modeling, which ensures your models remain mathematically sound and logically consistent, preventing common practitioner errors.

tasks: Evaluate a provided model summary for violations of hierarchy.
Correct a 'bad' model by re-adding missing main effects.

keyPoints: The Hierarchy Principle defined
Risks of omitting main effects
Model selection with interactions
Logical consistency in feature engineering

lectures.title: Practical Diagnostic Workflow
lectures.description: This lecture synthesizes the unit's concepts into a step-by-step checklist for cleaning and validating a multiple regression model.

sessions.title: The Multi-Step Diagnostic Checklist
sessions.description: This session teaches you a systematic workflow for checking VIF, adding interactions, and checking residual health in sequence. You will walk away with a professional-grade protocol for refining models, bridging the gap between textbook knowledge and real-world data science practice.

tasks: Sequence a series of diagnostic tests for a new dataset.
Propose a fix for a model with high VIF and non-linear patterns.

keyPoints: Exploratory correlation matrices
Sequential VIF testing
Hypothesizing interactions
Model refinement iteration loop

projects.stage_description: Detect and resolve multicollinearity issues (e.g., between 'Total Rooms' and 'Living Area') by calculating Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) and refining your feature selection.
projects.deliverable_increment: A VIF report and a refined feature list that eliminates redundant information.

exams.title: Complexity and Interaction Assessment
exams.goal: Evaluate the learner's ability to diagnose multicollinearity and correctly implement interaction terms in a multi-variable context.
sections: This comprehensive exam covers the detection of multicollinearity via VIF, the mathematical and conceptual interpretation of interaction terms, and the application of the hierarchy principle in model building.
successCriteria: Correctly identify redundant variables using VIF thresholds.
Accurately calculate the slope of a variable given an interaction effect.
Justify the inclusion of main effects alongside interactions.
Explain the impact of multicollinearity on model stability and p-values.

units.title: Robustness and Regularization: Moving Toward Modern DS
units.description: An introduction to Ridge and Lasso regression as 'anchors' that prevent models from overreacting to noise in high-dimensional data.

lectures.title: The Price of Complexity: The Bias-Variance Tradeoff
lectures.description: Before introducing solutions, we must understand the fundamental tension between a model's flexibility and its ability to generalize to new data.

sessions.title: Complexity and Overfitting
sessions.description: This session introduces the concept of overfitting through the lens of model complexity, teaching you how a model that follows data points too closely captures noise rather than signals. You will learn to identify the symptoms of a 'high-variance' model, which is a critical skill for moving from academic exercises to real-world datasets where noise is prevalent.

tasks: Sketch a high-degree polynomial fit vs. a linear fit and identify which captures noise.
Predict how a high-variance model would perform on a fresh test dataset.

keyPoints: Signal vs. noise in data
Definition of overfitting
The impact of model complexity on training error
Visualization of high-variance models

sessions.title: The Bias-Variance Decomposition
sessions.description: In this session, we formally decompose total error into bias and variance, explaining the mathematical trade-off that occurs when you simplify or complicate a model. You will gain the ability to reason about where a model sits on this spectrum, allowing you to make strategic decisions about model selection based on the volume and quality of your data.

tasks: Label a bullseye diagram with examples of high bias/low variance and low bias/high variance.
Calculate total error given hypothetical values for bias, variance, and irreducible error.

keyPoints: Definition of Bias in regression
Definition of Variance in regression
The decomposition of Mean Squared Error
Finding the optimal complexity 'sweet spot'

lectures.title: Shrinkage Methods: Ridge and Lasso
lectures.description: We introduce regularization as a mathematical penalty on large coefficients, effectively 'anchoring' the model to prevent extreme fluctuations.

sessions.title: Ridge Regression and the L2 Penalty
sessions.description: This session covers Ridge regression, explaining how adding a squared penalty term to the OLS cost function shrinks coefficients toward zero. You will understand how this 'L2 norm' stabilizes models in the presence of multicollinearity, fulfilling your goal of building robust models that don't overreact to specific features.

tasks: Write the Ridge cost function by adding the penalty term to the OLS objective.
Describe the effect on coefficients as the tuning parameter lambda increases.

keyPoints: The Ridge penalty term (L2 norm)
The role of the hyperparameter lambda
Impact on coefficient magnitude
Geometric intuition of the Ridge constraint

sessions.title: Lasso Regression and Feature Selection
sessions.description: We explore Lasso regression and its unique L1 penalty, which can force coefficients to be exactly zero. You will learn how Lasso acts as an automated feature selection tool, enabling you to simplify complex models and identify the most impactful predictors in high-dimensional datasets.

tasks: Compare the L1 and L2 penalty shapes geometrically.
Identify a scenario where Lasso would be preferred over Ridge for model interpretability.

keyPoints: The Lasso penalty term (L1 norm)
Sparsity and why Lasso sets coefficients to zero
Difference between L1 and L2 geometry
Interpretability benefits of Lasso

lectures.title: Tuning and Validation: Finding the Right Balance
lectures.description: Learn the practical workflow for selecting the best regularization strength using modern cross-validation techniques.

sessions.title: Cross-Validation for Lambda Selection
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to use K-fold cross-validation to choose the optimal value for the tuning parameter lambda. You will learn the 'Goldilocks' principle of model tuning, ensuring you don't over-regularize (underfit) or under-regularize (overfit), which is essential for production-ready practitioners.

tasks: Draw the process of K-fold cross-validation.
Interpret a plot of cross-validated error vs. log(lambda) to pick the best model.

keyPoints: Concept of K-fold cross-validation
Grid search for hyperparameters
The one-standard-error rule
Validation sets vs. Test sets

sessions.title: The Road Ahead: From Regression to Modern ML
sessions.description: In the final session of the course, we synthesize everything from the best-fit line to regularization, situating linear regression within the broader machine learning landscape. You will see how the foundations you've built lead directly into advanced topics like Elastic Net and Logistic Regression, giving you a clear roadmap for your continued growth as a data scientist.

tasks: Summarize the transition from simple OLS to regularized MLR.
Identify which course concepts apply to non-linear modeling.

keyPoints: Brief introduction to Elastic Net
Regression as the foundation for Neural Networks
Scaling laws and data requirements
Course summary and next steps

projects.stage_description: Finalize the project by implementing Lasso and Ridge regression to handle noise and potential overfitting. You will use cross-validation to find the optimal 'Alpha' parameter and compare the performance against your standard OLS model.
projects.deliverable_increment: Finalized model pipeline utilizing Lasso/Ridge regression and a model comparison summary (R-squared/RMSE) against the unregularized version.

exams.title: Unit 7 Comprehensive Exam: Robustness and Regularization
exams.goal: Evaluate the learner's ability to navigate the bias-variance tradeoff and correctly apply Ridge/Lasso techniques.
sections: This exam covers the bias-variance tradeoff, the mathematical and conceptual differences between L1 and L2 penalties, and the use of cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning.
successCriteria: Can define bias and variance and their relationship to model complexity.
Can distinguish between Ridge and Lasso penalties and their effects on coefficients.
Can interpret a cross-validation plot to select an optimal lambda value.
Can explain why regularization is necessary for high-dimensional or noisy data.
